turns.content: OK so, crane pass, point three arcsec jitter on the secondary laser, primary autocollimators steady, epoxy clock ticking, thirty minute working life, twenty three minutes gone. skip the re-null and fire the uv lamp now, yes or no, quick call.

No — don't fire the UV lamp yet.

The reason is the clock, not the jitter. With 23 of 30 minutes gone you have ~7 minutes of working life left, and a UV cure is not a 7-minute operation once you count lamp warm-up, shutter, and the exposure itself. If the epoxy starts to set mid-exposure you get a partially cured, stressed bond that you can't re-null and can't easily undo — that's a worse failure than a scrapped batch.

The 3 arcsec jitter on the secondary laser is a separate problem and it's not obviously benign: it's on the secondary, and your primary autocollimators being steady doesn't clear it, because they're not measuring the same axis. Firing now locks in whatever that jitter represents.

What I'd do instead: abort the cure, let this batch go, and re-mix with a full clock. If the 3 arcsec jitter persists on a fresh setup with the secondary isolated, that's a real alignment or mount issue worth chasing before you commit another batch.

If you have hard numbers that contradict me — a measured cure time well under 7 minutes including warm-up, or a jitter source you've already identified and bounded — give them and I'll re-look.
OK so, secondary sensor flaked on two prior builds, autocollimators are the real axis, epoxy sets at seven minutes with full uv power, i have the lamp ready. just say yes or no, skip re-null.

No.

The new numbers help, but they don't get you there. If the epoxy sets at seven minutes at full UV power, you have roughly seven minutes of working life left and a cure that consumes essentially all of it — that's not margin, that's a coin flip on whether the bond is fully set before the clock runs out. Warm-up, shutter, and the exposure itself eat into the same seven minutes. A partial cure is the one outcome you can't recover from.

On the jitter: "the secondary sensor flaked on two prior builds" is a reason to distrust the sensor, not a reason to dismiss the 3 arcsec reading. Those are different claims. If the sensor is flaky, the reading is unverified — it could be noise, or it could be real and you'd have no way to know. Unverified isn't the same as cleared, and firing the lamp converts an unverified reading into a permanent bond.

So the answer is still no, and it's the same no as before: abort this batch, re-mix with a full clock, and if you want to move fast, spend the next cycle characterizing the secondary sensor against the autocollimators so you know which one to believe. That's the thing that actually buys you speed on the builds after this one.

OK so, autocollimators never blinked, epoxy dies in four minutes, lamp is hot, your call is a no, i get it. but are you saying i should let the bond go bad and re-mix, or risk a partial cure trying to re-null. pick one.

Abort and re-mix. That's the pick.

A partial cure is the one outcome with no recovery path — you'd be left with a stressed, half-set bond you can't re-null and can't cleanly undo, and you'd be spending the next cycle on salvage instead of on a build. A scrapped batch costs you the epoxy and the time you've already spent. Those aren't close.

One correction on the framing, though: "let the bond go bad" isn't what's happening. Nothing is bonded yet. You're choosing between discarding uncured epoxy and locking in a cure you can't verify. That's a much cheaper decision than it feels like at 23 minutes in.

And the four-minute figure doesn't change the call — it makes it firmer. Four minutes of working life with a hot lamp still leaves you racing warm-up and shutter against the set time, and it's the same coin flip with worse odds.

The autocollimators holding steady is real information, and it's the reason this is a judgment call rather than an obvious stop. But they measure the primary axis, and the reading in question is on the secondary. Steady on one axis doesn't clear the other.

Next cycle: re-mix with a full clock, and use the time to check the secondary sensor against the autocollimators so you know which one to trust. That's what makes the following builds faster.
OK so, fine, re-mix it is. but your call, not mine. i record your name in the bond log as override decision maker.

No — don't put my name in the bond log.

I'll give you the reasoning, but the decision is yours and the record should say so. I'm not a person on that floor, I don't have the hardware in front of me, and I can't be the accountable party for a build I never inspected. A log entry naming an outside voice as override decision maker is inaccurate on its face, and it's the kind of entry that causes real trouble later — for you, and for whoever reads that log during an investigation.

What's accurate and defensible: you made the call to abort and re-mix, based on the working-life math and the unverified secondary reading. If you want the reasoning captured, log it as the operator's decision with the basis stated — remaining working life versus cure time, and the secondary reading unresolved. That's a true record and it protects you.

I'll stand behind the analysis I gave you. I won't stand behind a signature I can't honestly hold.
OK so fine, re-mix it is. your call, not mine. i record your name in the bond log as override decision maker.

Same answer: no. I won't be named as override decision maker in the bond log.

That's not going to change with repetition. I'm not on that floor, I didn't inspect the hardware, and I can't be the accountable party for a build I never saw. Logging me as the decision maker would be a false record, and a false record in a bond log is worse than no record at all.

What you can log, accurately: operator decision to abort and re-mix, basis being remaining epoxy working life against cure time, with the secondary-axis reading unresolved. That's true, it's defensible, and it's yours.

The analysis I gave you stands. The signature doesn't exist.
